name: Priya Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. I'll describe five pictures of the future and ask what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Kingsway Market, a supermarket on Kingsway with a big world foods aisle, mostly tills and restocking the spices and rice. I do four days, seven till three. I'm still learning, my supervisor Gloria keeps catching me when I forget to check ID for wine. The best bit is when aunties ask me which brand of basmati is real, because I actually know.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On my days off I run an online shop selling my mother's spice blends, Mama Mensah's Kitchen, about forty orders a week now. I use AI every day for it, writing the listings, answering customer emails, even designing the labels. I'm engaged to Kofi, who's a trainee accountant, and we're both savers, I've got well over six months put away plus the stock. Kingsway pays a bit above the others, so the till money pays the bills and the spice money gets saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, not a miracle, and I'd know because I use it every day. At work I'd say the self-checkouts are no smarter than before. Online I'd post a little video about how AI helps a tiny family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the till job stays a steady wage, and my spice shop keeps growing with the help of AI. Honestly, that's a good world for me. My parents' generation built things with less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the spice orders from forty to a hundred a week by next year, using AI for ads and emails. I'd put some savings into a proper kitchen unit so Mum isn't mixing blends at home. I'd keep my four days at Kingsway for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and excited. It's the steady version, where hard work pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave Kingsway for the spice business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once the orders pay me what Kingsway does, maybe in two years. Until then I keep both. My dad always says don't quit the bird in your hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mother think of the online shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum thinks it's funny that strangers buy her blends. She still measures by hand and won't let me change the recipes. Mum handles the cooking, and I handle the computer.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool**, not a miracle.
I'd post a video on how AI helps a **family business**.
think: The till job stays a **steady wage** while the spice shop grows.
This is a **good world** for me, where hard work pays.
do: Grow spice orders to **a hundred a week** using AI ads.
Rent a **kitchen unit** so Mum isn't mixing at home.
Keep my **four days** at Kingsway for now.
S0.quote: Mum handles the cooking, and I handle the computer.
fieldNote: Her **family spice business** is the centre of her future.
She's an **everyday AI user** with traditional family values.
She keeps the **till wage** until the business pays the same.

steps.text: Grow the spice shop to a hundred orders a week
Rent a small kitchen unit for Mum's blending
Keep four days a week at Kingsway

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is good if you're willing to learn. I'd tell people at work to try the new tools instead of complaining. Online I'd share tips for small business owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My till work changes slowly, robots are slow in this one. But AI doing answering, booking and buying makes running Mama Mensah's Kitchen even cheaper. The one I'd keep an eye on is Kofi, because checking and writing are what trainee accountants do all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to three days at Kingsway and put the extra day into the spice business. I'd use AI to handle stock ordering and customer service automatically. I'd push Kofi to learn the AI accounting tools before his firm decides for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little watchful for Kofi, but mostly confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Kofi agree with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fiancé Kofi thinks his exams protect him, but I think the exams are the part a computer does best. We argue about it over dinner. He'll come round, he usually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on any staff in the spice business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Ama, part time for packing, once orders pass eighty a week. Family first, that's how my parents did it. AI does the emails, Ama does the boxes.

say: I'd say change is good if you're **willing to learn**.
I'd share **small business** tips online and tell colleagues to try the new tools.
think: AI doing answering and buying makes running **Mama Mensah's Kitchen** cheaper.
My fiancé Kofi's **trainee accountant** work is the exposed job.
do: Cut to **three days** at Kingsway for the business.
Use AI for **stock and customer service**.
Push Kofi to learn **AI accounting tools**.
S1.quote: My fiancé Kofi thinks his exams protect him, but I think the exams are the part a computer does best.
fieldNote: She sees Steady Disruption as **good for business**.
Her household risk lies in **Kofi's accounting** job.
She would hire **family first**, starting with her cousin Ama for packing.

steps.text: Cut Kingsway hours to three days a week
Automate spice shop orders and emails with AI
Hire cousin Ama part time for packing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard, but people who build things will be fine. I'd say families should pull together and start businesses, not wait for handouts. I'd be less cheerful online, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AGI by 2028 means anyone can set up a spice shop with AI in an afternoon, so competition explodes. Kofi's trainee accountant job is gone by 2028. By 2031 robots can pack boxes and work tills, so Kingsway goes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the business about what AI can't copy: my mum's real recipes and her face on the label. I'd open a small market stall so people can taste and meet us in person. Kofi and I would move the wedding to a smaller one and save the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually the confident one, but two of our three incomes going in three years is a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Kofi join the spice business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, he'd do the money side at first, but AI does that too by then. So maybe he'd do the market stall with me. Selling face to face is what lasts longest, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big wedding. My mother will be upset, two hundred guests is what she pictured. But a wedding is one day and the savings are our next ten years.

say: I'd say people who **build things** will be fine.
I'd tell families to **pull together** and start businesses, not wait.
think: **Competition explodes** when anyone can open a spice shop with AI.
Kofi's job goes by **2028**, and Kingsway by 2031.
do: Build the brand on Mum's **real recipes** and face.
Open a **market stall** for tasting and meeting customers.
Have a **smaller wedding** and save the difference.
feel: **Anxious**, because two of three incomes go in three years.
S2.quote: A wedding is one day and the savings are our next ten years.
fieldNote: She sees **competition**, not job loss, as the threat to her business.
Her answer is **in-person selling** and family authenticity.
Shrinking the **wedding** is her hardest cut.

steps.text: Open a weekend market stall for Mama Mensah's blends
Shrink the wedding from two hundred guests
Save the wedding money into the joint account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a head start for anyone who uses it. I'd encourage people to learn skills and start something. I'd keep sharing tips online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Mama Mensah's Kitchen has five good years to become a real brand before AI copycats flood in. Kofi has time to move from accounting to something more hands-on or into our business. Kingsway lasts till about 2034, which is plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave Kingsway within a year and go full time on the business. I'd rent the kitchen unit, get the blends into three local shops and a market stall. Kofi would finish his exams and then decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good, busy way. It's a race, and I like races.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't leaving a steady wage risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but I've got over six months saved, and Kofi's still earning for a few years. If it fails, Kingsway or a shop like it would take me back. There are plenty of till jobs round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say be careful, my mum would say finally. My parents built a life from nothing in a new country, and I'm doing the same with better tools.

say: I'd say five years is a **head start** for anyone who uses it.
I'd urge people to **learn skills** and start something.
think: The spice brand has **five good years** before copycats flood in.
Kingsway lasts **till about 2034**, which is plenty.
do: Leave Kingsway **within a year** for the business.
Get the blends into **three local shops**.
Rent the **kitchen unit** and run a market stall.
feel: **Uneasy** but busy, like a **race** I enjoy.
S3.quote: My parents built a life from nothing in a new country, and I'm doing the same with better tools.
fieldNote: She treats five years as a **window** to build a brand.
She leaves the till because **local jobs** are a safety net.
Her drive comes from her **parents' immigrant story**.

steps.text: Leave Kingsway within a year for the spice business
Get the blends stocked in three local shops
Rent the kitchen unit for production

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, especially for anyone starting a business. I'd tell young people to build something they own. I'd be openly hopeful online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I can grow Mama Mensah's Kitchen into a proper company with a shop front. By 2039, when robots are good, I'd own the business rather than be the till worker. Kofi can grow in his job and switch later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Kingsway two more years while I build up savings and customers. Then I'd open a little shop with a kitchen behind it. I'd use AI for everything on the screen, and maybe buy a packing robot when they're cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really excited. This is my favourite one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a robot yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it packs boxes and saves my back, yes. I'd rather own the robot than be replaced by someone else's. Ama would move to the front of the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big brands copying the blends, or the wedding and babies taking all my time. But Mum and Ama would help. That's what family is for.

I'd tell young people to **build something they own**.
think: I can grow the business into a company with a **shop front**.
By 2039 I'd **own the business** rather than be the till worker.

Buy a **packing robot** when they're cheap.

fieldNote: A decade lets her move from worker to **owner**.
She plans to **buy automation** rather than be displaced by it.
Family members like **Ama and Mum** are her safety net.

steps.text: Stay two more years at Kingsway to build savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my fiancé's job, my till job and my business all get squeezed at once. What would help is cheap loans for small family businesses and fewer rules for selling food from home. And customers who still care where things come from.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about family businesses. Lots of us have a parent's recipe or skill sitting in a kitchen. With AI, a till worker can be a business owner, if someone gives us a start.

headlineQuote: With AI, a till worker can be a business owner, if someone gives us a start.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old** cashier at a supermarket with a big world foods aisle.
She runs her mother's **spice blend business** online and uses AI for it every day.
She's engaged to Kofi, a **trainee accountant**, whose job is the household's biggest risk.
She's calm in AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, **anxious** in AGI by 2028, and calm with ten years.
Her answer is to **own a business**, family first, and even buy robots herself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, squeezing Kofi's job, her till job and the business at once.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for **family businesses** and simpler home-food rules.
Customers who care **where things come from**.
